text:
North Korea Touts Successful Test of New Weapon of ‘Great Significance’

@LibertarianInst 

North Korea claims to have successfully tested a missile system it previously labeled as hypersonic. 

“The Missile Administration of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea successfully tested a new-type weapon, which is of great significance in the rapid technological development of weapon systems,” North Korean state media reported on Tuesday, noting the test occurred on Sunday. 

While the state media report did not identify the weapon as hypersonic, photos published by KCNA appeared to show the Hwasong-11Ma, which North Korea has previously described as a hypersonic missile.

According to KCNA, Supreme Leader Kim Un observed the test, remarking, “To acquire such a technology is of weighty significance in the state’s readiness for war and the future development of the armed forces.” He added, “The enemy will know better what such progress means without any explanation in the aspect of military technology,” and “such reality would give the enemy an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow.”

South Korea and Japan both reported that North Korea fired two missiles on Sunday. The test appears to have raised alarms in the US and among its allies in the region. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi warned reporters about the increasingly severe security situation in the region.

“Last year, there were four instances and at least five missiles, so the number of instances has doubled, and the number of missiles has increased to at least three times as many,” Koizumi said, describing the regional security situation as “growing increasingly severe.”

The test also prompted the US, Japan, and South Korea to hold an emergency call. Tensions have flared in the region following two rounds of US-led war games and North Korea’s concerns that Washington will assist Seoul and Tokyo in developing nuclear attack submarines. 

Over the past two months, the US has led two major rounds of war games in the region. In August, the US and South Korea held the bilateral Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises. Trump ordered the drills cut roughly in half, arguing they sent an unnecessarily hostile message to North Korea. However, the trilateral US-South Korea-Japan Freedom Edge exercises went forward as planned earlier this month.

Trump scaled back the war games as he offered to meet with Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un and predicted the two would meet later this year. However, Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, rebuked the overture, saying that merely scaling back the war games did not change the hostile US policy towards North Korea. 

Adding to the tensions in the region are moves by South Korea and Japan toward acquiring nuclear-powered submarines. Washington has approved Seoul’s plan to build nuclear-powered attack submarines, while the possibility of Japan acquiring similar vessels has also drawn support from a US Navy official.

In a commentary published by KCNA, international affairs analyst Choe Ju Hyon accused the US of instigating South Korea and Japan to acquire nuclear submarines. “The reality goes to prove that Washington’s plan for ‘AUKUS 2.0,’ which allows the transfer of nuclear technology for munitions to non-nuclear allies, has entered the phase of full-scale expansion,” he wrote.

AUKUS is a trilateral pact between the US, the UK, and Australia. Under the deal, the US and UK agreed to help Australia build a fleet of nuclear submarines. China has also criticized the transfer of nuclear-propulsion technology under AUKUS. The Chinese Foreign Ministry said AUKUS “undermine[s] strategic stability and provoke[s] an arms race in the region.”

In his article, Choe argued that North Korea must increase its nuclear deterrent in response to South Korea and Japan acquiring nuclear submarines. North Korea must “bolster up its nuclear war deterrent means both in quality and quantity without the slightest stagnation and stalemate.”

text:
Guru Nanga Tales: The UN & The Question of Power (38/42)

A Note From the Observer

Mango had no vote. Mango submitted a sentence anyway, on the grounds that observers at the UN do this constantly and it has never once been stopped.

Mango's sentence was not from a leader. It was the Secretary-General's description of his own job, the week before: no army, no intelligence service and not much money. Mango's reason: this is also the position of a cat in a New York apartment, and the apartment has been run from that position for six years without a single walkout, veto or emergency session. The humans come and go. The couch remains. Mango offered this not as advice but as a thing to consider.

Mango added three observations from the couch, in the order they occurred. First, that the only people who left the hall today were the ones being talked about, and the only people who stayed were the ones talking, and that this is how every room works and the UN had merely built a large one. Second, that the stream had shown 193 desks and one podium and no cat, and that the coverage of this institution has been incomplete since 1945. Third, that the pigeon was still there.

Guru Nanga ruled the sentence admissible and the vote inadmissible, since the rules said five judges and the rules are the rules, which had been the entire afternoon's argument. Mango accepted the ruling in the manner of a small country, which is to say completely and without any change in behaviour.

Mango asked one last question, which was whether the towel was saffron. Guru Nanga said it was green. Mango said it looked saffron on the video. Guru Nanga said the video was wrong, and that this would be the last time a screen in New York was wrong about something in California today, though not the last time a screen in New York was wrong.

Ben asked whether Mango would be attending future debates. Guru Nanga said Mango had never attended this one. Mango had been present, informed and not allowed to vote, and there is a chair for that in the actual building, and it is called the observer's chair, and it is also, in every practical sense, a couch.

text:
Halloween: The Game
Ideas & Changes

Call me an unusual. Michael Myers should never be nurfed. The advantage always goes to the attacker and rarely to the defenders. The Trojan Horse proved this historically. With this type of game, you cannot save everyone and Myers should always have the advantage over the player heros and NPCs. I am almost always against a nerf for the Killer. If you want a nerfed killer, go back to Dead By Daylight.

While playing this game for a few days. I have thought out some map and enviromental changes.

1. The map(s) should be increased in size. Even if its offered as an option select at menu. A greater Haddonfield, Illinois. Larger map means bigger oppertunities for the Killer and players. 

2. Each NPC victims need a daily habit and routine to keep every map fresh and harder for players. 

3. Increasing NPC victims to 13 total targets.

4. As maps (DLC) are introduced, so should enviroments, characters, maps, weapons, kills, etc. of the franchise should be introduced.

5. More masks and costumes for Myers from the Halloween franchise.

6. An increase to the powers of Myers. Examples: 

Fog Creation: An Exagerated fog just like the old horror movies. A crawling fog that covers a large area, causing blinding fear and uncertainty to victims and players.

Clone: Appearing in multiple locations (Tempory). It is designed as a scare tactic against players. Visualize yourself, looting a house or rounding a corner, suddenly Michael appears, spots you, suddenly vanishes. Increases the terrified mechanic, potentially scaring NPCs including players.

Blend: Michael should have a passive to blend in with the world. Especially while he observes his target(s). Even in a crowded area.

7. Each map should have NPCs fillers. These vary as a Michael Myers copycats, 
Varieties also should include pranksters, drunkards, party goer, cry wolf, costume dressers, and regular looking suburban pedestrians. They cannot be harmed or call police. They are reactionary to spotting either dead body or witnessing a kill. They will fill the streets and fill the greater Haddonfield. In addition a Dynamic NPC event from fillers. Once Myers accumulates 16 body kill count, the Myers house is surrounded, looted and vandilized.

8. If the entire police force is eliminated, a small posse is formed.

9. Dynamic Weather patterns that hinder NPCs and Players, excluding Myers. These patterns will deafen or blind depending. These should hinder movement, trick of the eye, etc. Playing on the scare tactic of a Killer Myers may or may not be present.

10. In addition to the 3 priority targets. Michael should have a rare oppertunity to kill a unique target. An NPC such as Judith Myers, a relative, or a player. This is only revealed to Myers in vacinity. A "Marked for Death" just like the movies... If it is a marked player, they should not get a giant UI banner the whole match; the dread is in not knowing.

11. Current Maps: 4 Dogs 

Greater Haddonfield: 7-8 Dogs should be added as a general threat against a stealthy Myers and alert NPCs / players. They bark at Myers at close range, wake sleeping NPCs, and can draw player attention. They are an alarm system that punishes sloppy stalking. Dogs can be killed like the movies and should not generate 1% bloodlust build, if any at all.

12. In addition to the many hiding spots already given. I propose beds should be another hiding spot.

13. Bicycles should have the capacity for a second rider.

14. In a private lobby: There should be an AI controlled Michael Myers, toggled by difficulty. So players can hone their civillian skills.

THE SCRIPTURES HAD FORETOLD THAT ONE OF the prominent marks of Anti-Christ would be the enforcement of vows of celibacy on its religious orders and hierarchy: " The Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; speaking lies in hypocrisy;-forbidding to marry..." (1 Time. 4:1-2). Does not Catholicism teach, rather, forbid  all of its priests and nuns "to marry"?

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

Across 39 main-board IPOs, 86% of the applications came in on the last of the three days the issue stayed open.

HOW TO READ IT
Each pale line is one IPO, tracked from its first minute to its last. The bold line is the average of all 39 IPOs placed on top of each other. Where a pale line stays flat early and shoots up at the end, that IPO was mostly bid on day three.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Day 1 averaged just 5% of bids, while day 2 averaged 14%, and day 3 averaged 86%, so the curve bends sharply on the final day.
- 38 of the 39 IPOs had more than half of their applications on the last day, which is why so many pale lines crowd the right edge.
- 19 IPOs had their biggest day before day 3, then picked up again to finish over 1x, the common U-shape of a slow start and a late rush.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Source: exchange IPO application data, read every hour while each IPO was open. 39 main-board IPOs that opened and closed between 29 Jul and 21 Sep 2026, each open for three days. Every IPO is put on the same axes: time as a share of its own open hours (10 am to 5 pm on each of its three days), demand as a share of its own closing figure, so issues of different sizes and lengths can be averaged. A reading above the closing figure is a bad refresh and is dropped (7 of 959); after that each point carries the highest reading so far. Every figure quoted is read at the end of a day, where a real reading sits; nothing between two readings is estimated. The end of every curve is the exchange's own closing figure. Left out: 401 main-board IPOs that closed before our hourly readings begin (25 Jul), 6 that stayed open longer than three days and cannot share this axis, and all 50 SME issues, which run on a separate board and are never averaged in here. This is what 39 IPOs already closed did. It says nothing about any IPO still to come.

HOW THE DEMAND BUILT UP (average of 39 IPOs, 29 Jul to 21 Sep 2026)
End of day one: 5% of the final applications were in.
End of day two: 14%.
Final day: the other 86%.
38 of the 39 got more than half their applications on that last day.

19 of the 39 had fewer applications than shares on offer at the end of day one. All 19 finished with more. Rays of Belief sat at 0.9x on day one and finished at 128x.

text:
Kirby Smart is trying to get one of his receivers off the field. He cannot do it.

"I keep trying to take him off to save money and it's not working."

The player is London Humphreys, and this is the strangest NIL story of the year.

Humphreys grew up in Nashville and went to Christ Presbyterian Academy. He was a three star. His offers were Vanderbilt, Memphis, Middle Tennessee State and Minnesota.

He picked Vanderbilt, and as a true freshman in 2023 he scored in his college debut. Against Wake Forest he went for 109 yards and a touchdown and was named SEC Freshman of the Week.

He finished that season with 439 yards and four touchdowns. He made the SEC All Freshman team. He was one of three freshmen in the entire conference with four or more receiving touchdowns.

Then he transferred to Georgia.

And he basically stopped catching the ball.

In three seasons in Athens he has 35 catches. Total. 531 yards, six touchdowns.

This year, through three games, he has 2 catches for 11 yards.

Here is the part that makes it interesting.

Almost every NIL incentive in college football is tied to production. Catches. Yards. Touchdowns. Playing time on offense.

Humphreys has a clause in his deal that pays him more for special teams snaps.

Not returns. Coverage. The part of the game nobody wants.

So he fights to be out there on every one of them, and every one of them costs Georgia money, and his head coach cannot talk him out of it.

Against Arkansas he came free off the edge and blocked a punt in the third quarter. The ball traveled 14 yards.

Smart on him this week.

"He cares so much. He's the highest-character kid on the team. He's one of the best blockers."

And then the punchline.

"He's worth it."

Now the honest part. He is getting paid for this. It is an incentive, and it is working exactly the way an incentive is supposed to work.

But somebody had to agree to build the deal that way.

A kid who was All Freshman in the SEC at 18 looked at a roster full of five star receivers, understood he was not going to be the guy, and tied his money to the ugliest job on the field instead of transferring again.

He is a senior now. He says his job is teaching the young receivers how to do it.

Most guys chase the ball. This one chased the coverage unit.

I’ll respond to Selbrede myself. Stephen Wolfe made the point “(1) that each of us has a people-group (i.e., an ethnicity), (2) that each people-group can be conscious of itself, and (3) that each people-group has a right to be for itself. These last two elements are essential to nationalism.” 

Martin Selbrede countered this by denying that governments should even regulate language to protect national particularity! He appeals to Isaiah 19:18, which predicts that five cities in Egypt will speak Hebrew. This is the foolish libertarianism that is sadly too common among Reconstructionists. Greg Bahnsen even said that the government is not biblically authorized to outlaw the making and distribution of porn.

Isaiah 2:2 (in response to Selbrede) is not about philology in general. One meaning is that since the time of Alexander there were communities of Jews living in Egypt. They even had their own temple at Memphis, Leontopolis actually, close to modern Cairo, called the Temple of Onias. Onias justified its construction to Ptolemy on the basis of Isaiah 19:19 (“In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the heart of Egypt”). It was staffed by Levitical priests and offered sacrifices until Vespasian ordered its demolition in 73 AD. But there’s also an eschatological perspective on Isaiah 19:18-21, where the “language of Canaan” refers to the language of repentance, the “pure speech” of Zeph. 3:9.

The proclamation of the gospel is why Psalm 87 shows a multitude of nations born in Zion. It’s why Japheth dwells in the tents of Shem in Gen. 9:27. It’s why Isaiah 2 shows all the nations flowing into the house of the Lord.

Like many other Alienists, Selbrede acknowledges that the existence of discrete nations is acceptable, but not if these nations self-consciously remain discrete and exclusive. He sees in Isaiah 19:23 a “remarkably porous” border between Egypt and Assyria. This is because spiritual unity leads to good will and commerce among nations. This is how European civilization was formed. We’re still commanded to prioritize our own in 1 Tim. 5:8. And when we do, Alienists shriek that this is sinful division within the body of Christ. 

But we see in Acts 6:1 just the opposite. When the early church was growing so fast that linguistic and ethnonational differences were drawing accusations of impartiality against the apostles, the solution was segregation! Hellenist deacons, including Stephen, were appointed to govern the daily distribution to their own people.

And notice that 1 Tim. 5:8 is specifically in the context of charity for widows. Special care for one’s own is directly linked to segregation.

text:
Pat Ryan's Formal Break With Israel

From a conservative perspective, Pat Ryan’s break with AIPAC in July 2026 is not merely a lone moderate's disagreement with Benjamin Netanyahu. Instead, it is viewed as part of a broader trend already evident in figures like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed. This trend reflects a growing willingness to treat the U.S.-Israel security relationship as optional or illegitimate and to view AIPAC as a corrupting influence rather than just another American interest group.

Conservatives who defend the U.S.-Israel alliance typically start from two key premises: First, they see Israel as a democratic partner on the front lines against Iran-backed militias. Second, they consider AIPAC a transparent lobbying organization that represents American supporters of that partnership, rather than a covert “dark money” conspiracy. Within this framework, Ryan, Mamdani, and El-Sayed represent different positions along a continuum.

Ryan previously funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars through AIPAC channels, traveled to Israel on related trips, and voted for the pro-aid consensus. However, he later joined 103 House Democrats in supporting the Massie amendment, which sought to strip $3.3 billion in military assistance to Israel. He condemned the Israeli government as a “corrupt and increasingly dangerous Netanyahu regime” and declared that he no longer wanted AIPAC’s endorsement or financial support. Opponents in his district characterized this shift as a late conversion influenced by the party's left wing, which was redefining the standards of acceptability.

Mamdani took his criticisms further in both rhetoric and foundational beliefs. He referred to AIPAC as “monsters” who move “millions in dark money” to protect their influence, sustain Netanyahu’s wars, and divide Americans. This language was condemned by Jewish organizations and hundreds of rabbis as a resurgence of classic dual-loyalty and shadowy-control stereotypes. Additionally, he declined to recognize Israel as a Jewish state in the traditional sense, stating that he only supports a state of “equal rights” and will not endorse any state that “privileges one religion.” This stance represents a more fundamental objection than Ryan’s announced shift.

El-Sayed made AIPAC a central target in his statewide campaign, labeling its spending as “legalized bribery” and arguing that U.S. aid to Israel should be redirected to Michigan rather than used for “bombs on other people and their kids.” He managed to win the Democratic Senate nomination despite AIPAC and allied groups spending tens of millions of dollars against him, with a platform that included stopping weapons shipments. Conservatives viewed his campaign as placing the lobby itself on the ballot and reframing Israeli aid as a form of domestic theft rather than a security commitment.

Many conservatives see a significant divide among these three figures rather than convergence. While Ryan still offers the conventional caveats—supporting Israel’s right to exist, denouncing Hamas as terrorists, and opposing antisemitism—Mamdani and El-Sayed often treat these issues as secondary or use them as political cover. For this reason, some conservatives describe Ryan as a "weathervane" rather than an ideologue: he accepted support from AIPAC when it was beneficial and then distanced himself once Democratic primary voters and activist networks shifted. In contrast, Mamdani and El-Sayed are viewed as genuine representatives of the left, with connections to groups like DSA, SJP, and, in El-Sayed’s case, endorsements from JVP.

The conservative comparison, therefore, is not that the three men sound identical. Rather, Ryan’s vote, coupled with his repudiation, shows how much the party's center of gravity has already shifted. A previously AIPAC-endorsed Democrat from the Hudson Valley now utilizes the same tactics: cutting aid, personalizing the Israeli government as a “regime,” and treating AIPAC as politically toxic. In this narrative, Mamdani and El-Sayed are seen as the vanguard of a movement, while Ryan's actions indicate that this vanguard is no longer limited to safely progressive districts.

The strategic concern follows logically from this perspective. From this view, all three individuals weaken a U.S. ally while Iran, Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis remain active. They do this by targeting the most organized American advocate for the alliance. Conservatives note that similar ethnic or foreign-policy PACs rarely attract the same level of scrutiny; the focus on AIPAC appears selective. Ryan’s request for a refund of approximately $790,000 raised during Jackie Auringer’s challenge is cited as a practical test: if his split is a matter of principle, then he should return the money collected under a different set of promises.

text:
Poker as a test of Jev. How does Jev compare with a deterministic poker solver (TexasSolver)?

I'm not knowledgable enough in poker but I'm quoting the beginning of this piece so you all can decide whether you want to click through and read the whole thing.

"1. The setup: I solved one flop with TexasSolver: heads-up, 100bb deep, LJ opens and BTN calls, flop Q-spade 9-diamond 4-spade. Eight minutes, 7.6GB, 0.59% exploitability. That gives the correct strategy for every hand either player can hold, on every turn card, at every decision."

("bb" stands for "big blinds".)

"Jev gets a state object describing the table the way a player sees it, and one question: which action should hero take, from the options the solver's tree offers. Pot odds, stack-to-pot ratio, hero's hand rank and outs are computed in Python first, so Jev never does arithmetic."

"2. An easy spot: good. Hero holds J-spade T-spade on Q-spade 9-diamond 4-spade 2-heart facing a bet of 8 into 10.5. Fifteen outs, needs 30% equity to call, has 33%."

"Option: Solver vs Jev"
"Call 8: 96% vs 94%"
"Raise to 24: 4% vs 2%"
"All-in 95.5: 0% vs 2%"
"Fold: 0% vs 2%"

"Jev calls at 94%, the solver calls at 96%. 215ms. Across 30 random spots it matched the solver's top action 63% of the time."

He goes on to describe situations that Jev gets wrong. Then he goes on to add bits of information (such as revealing one of the opponent's cards) to Jev's input bit by bit to see how it improves Jev's probability.

Three F-15E Strike Eagles were lost to friendly fire over Kuwait in the opening weeks and a fourth was shot down over Iran.

The rescue mission that pulled those two crewmen out cost two MC-130Js and four Little Bird helicopters, all deliberately destroyed so Iran couldn't take them, making it the most expensive single operation of the war.

An E-3G Sentry sitting on the taxiway at Prince Sultan was cut in half by Iranian fire, and the only replacement is a plane that costs half a billion dollars.

Trump told NewsNation there was "no damage, no nothing" from the Jordan strikes that hit eight F-15s and an A-10.

Replacing all of it runs past $4 billion, and half the country's interceptors are gone with at least five years to rebuild them.

China builds 800 missiles a year and military leaders think it could move on Taiwan by 2027, which means if that fight comes, the drones, radar planes and interceptors America would need for it are already burned up in the Middle East.

text:
Guru Nanga Tales: The UN & The Question of Power (23/42)

Bigger Than Five (continued)

Qatar, being small, sent a Sandhurst graduate who chaired the 2006 Asian Games, sits on the Olympic committee and owns a Paris football club. Guru Nanga called him the Sports Commissioner. Last year he had said the fallback of the international order "in favor of the logic of power means paving the way for the law of the jungle." This morning he had said the core of the region's danger "is the absence of a regional collective security system" and offered his country as a "trusted mediator." Guru Nanga observed that a man who runs sporting events understands that the game only works if the fixture list is agreed in advance, and that the region has been playing friendlies for eighty years.

Egypt, being large, sent a note. Its leader was an infantry officer who ran military intelligence and attended the US Army War College, where he sometimes led Friday prayers. Guru Nanga called him the Intelligence Director. His prime minister led the delegation. The note, from Davos, said "international law and the UN charter should be respected" and repeated the word non-interference, and from the spring it added a wish to "extinguish the flames of war in the Gulf." Guru Nanga wrote down that an intelligence director speaks rarely and in complete sentences, and that this one had not said whose flames.

Guru Nanga tallied the row. A striker wanted the referee replaced, a sports commissioner wanted a fixture list, and an intelligence director wanted the fire out and did not say who had lit it. He noted that this is the same conversation held at every football club in the world, and that the region had been holding it with live ammunition.

text:
Guru Nanga Tales: The UN & The Question of Power (42/42)

A Statement From Guru Nanga to the Assorted Nuts (continued)

I alternated them, small and large, because that is how current travels and because it seemed fair. It was fair. It changed nothing. The large ones were still large when the small ones finished speaking, and the small ones were still right. I do not offer this as a finding. I offer it as the weather.

The man who asked the question leaves on December 31. He said the danger is not technology but technology without accountability, and I would extend that. The danger is not power. It is power without a chair to sit in, where somebody can read your speech back to you slowly, in your own voice, badly, while a cat in the actual city counts the people leaving.

That is the service we provide, Mango and I. The observer has the room. I have the bridge. Between us we have no army, no intelligence service and not much money, and the afternoon was still covered more completely than the stream managed. The nimbu pani is finished. The lemons were from Walnut Creek and travelled by cooler, unseized. The shadow has left the lawn.

The debate continues in the actual building through Monday, September 28, when New Zealand speaks last, and I would suggest, as a thing to consider, that you watch the ones who did not come as closely as the ones who did, and the ones who left more closely than either, and the one who goes last more closely than all of them, since by then the room will be honest about its size. text:
Guru Nanga Tales: The UN & The Question of Power (41/42)

A Statement From Guru Nanga to the Assorted Nuts

To the Assorted Nuts, from a hotel lawn in Redding, legs out, towel green, facing a bridge that is right one day a year and does not apologise for the other 364.

You asked for thoughts. You received a debate among twenty-six countries, taken small and large in turn, sixteen of which attended, ten of which sent notes, one of which walked out of the real building before I had finished reading its note, one of which will speak last on Monday and sent word early, and five judges, all of whom attended, which already puts you ahead of the Security Council on attendance and roughly level with it on agreement.

You voted five ways. Ben for rules. Val for limits. Nitin for friends with weapons. Burton for inaction, professionally assessed. Neil for a crossroads with one large truck. None of you voted for force, and none of you has an army, so the two facts may be related. I do not offer this as advice. I offer it as a thing to consider the next time one of you proposes settling a group-chat dispute by a show of strength.

The Secretary-General asked who has power, who is denied it, how it is used and how it is changing. Here is where the afternoon left it. Power is held by the people who were mostly not in the room. It is denied to the people who spoke most clearly about the rules, and to one island that spoke about them in the dark. It is used with the law by those who can afford lawyers and beyond the law by those who can afford not to. And it is changing hands, toward companies, machines and whoever crosses the intersection first, with or without notice.

text:
Guru Nanga Tales: The UN & The Question of Power (40/42)

Guru Nanga's Ten Takeaways (continued)

Six. The sentence with the longest shelf life came from the comedian: no guarantees except friends and weapons. It has held for four and a half years and nobody offered a replacement.

Seven. Power is moving from governments to a handful of companies and machines, and the two men who agreed on this most clearly, the Refugee Accountant and the Tower Landlord, agreed on nothing else. When opposites share a fact, consider the fact.

Eight. Sovereignty without technological agency is dependency in practice, said the man who once sold chickens beside a highway. This applies to households, utilities and islands as well as continents, and it is the only item on this list with an engineering solution. The Long-Haired Engineering Lecturer would know the equations. He does not currently have the voltage.

Nine. The unanimous decisions are the slow ones. The Assembly agreed in 1995 that the enemy-state clauses were obsolete and they are still in the Charter. Agreement is not action. A bridge that is right one day a year has a better record, and it has never held a session.

Ten. The man with no army asked the question, and the five judges, who also have no army, answered it better than the twenty-six who do. The observer, who has no army, no vote and a couch, answered it better than the judges. This is not a coincidence. It is what happens as the microphone gets further from the weapon.

A list of ten is itself a display of power. Nobody asked for the tenth one. Mango had asked for none of them and had received all ten, which Mango logged as coercion and Guru Nanga logged as a newsletter.

text:
On This Day in Holocaust History — September 22

1933—Nazi Germany enacted the Reich Culture Chamber Law, establishing the Reich Chamber of Culture under Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels.
The organization controlled seven fields: literature, journalism, radio, theater, music, film, and the visual arts. Anyone wishing to work professionally in German cultural life was required to belong to the appropriate chamber.
    Jews and people whose art or political beliefs the Nazis considered unacceptable were denied membership, effectively destroying their careers. Books, music, paintings, plays, films, and news reporting were brought under ideological control.
    The persecution of Jewish culture was not incidental. By silencing Jewish writers, musicians, artists, actors, and journalists, the regime sought to remove Jewish voices from Germany’s collective memory before it attempted to remove Jewish people themselves.

September 22–23, 1938—British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain met Adolf Hitler at Bad Godesberg to continue negotiations over Czechoslovakia’s Sudetenland.
Britain and France had already pressured Czechoslovakia to surrender territory to Germany. Hitler now escalated his demands, insisting upon an almost immediate German occupation and rejecting the slower transfer Chamberlain believed they had discussed.
The crisis culminated in the Munich Agreement of September 29–30, reached without Czechoslovakia’s meaningful participation. Germany acquired Czechoslovakia’s border defenses and strategic industries. Tens of thousands of Jews fled the annexed territory, while those who remained came under Nazi racial rule.

1939—German forces formally handed Brest-Litovsk in occupied Poland to the Soviet Red Army. German and Soviet commanders observed a military ceremony marking the transfer of the city under the territorial division secretly arranged in the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact.
Poland was being partitioned between two dictatorships. Brest remained under Soviet rule until Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941. The Germans subsequently established a ghetto there and murdered most of the region’s Jewish population.

September 22–24, 1941—Thousands of Jews from Ejszyszki—today Eišiškės, Lithuania—and nearby communities remained imprisoned inside a synagogue and two houses of study.
They were held for at least three days without food, water, or sanitation. Some Jews had escaped or found hiding places when Lithuanian auxiliary police began the roundup on September 21, but most were trapped.
On September 25 and 26, German Einsatzkommando 3 personnel and Lithuanian auxiliaries took the prisoners to prepared killing sites and shot approximately 3,500 Jewish men, women, and children. In a matter of days, they destroyed a Jewish community that had existed for more than 250 years.

1941—German police formations and local auxiliaries carried out mass shootings of Jews in and around Vinnytsia, Ukraine. Older chronologies place the culmination of the killing operation on September 22 and estimate that approximately 28,000 people from Vinnytsia and surrounding communities were murdered during the September massacres.
Vinnytsia became one of the killing grounds of the “Holocaust by bullets”—the phase of the genocide in which entire communities were assembled, marched to pits, forced to surrender their clothing and possessions, and shot at close range.

1942—German SS and police forces began the destruction of the Częstochowa Ghetto in occupied Poland.
The deportations continued through October 8. Approximately 39,000 Jews were packed into freight cars and transported to the Treblinka extermination camp. Elderly residents and children from the ghetto’s orphanage were murdered locally.
Around 5,000 Jews considered capable of forced labor were confined in a smaller ghetto. Others escaped or hid. The surviving prisoners were subsequently exploited in German-controlled armaments factories, where forced labor temporarily postponed—but did not end—the threat of murder.

1942—The National Council of the Reformed Church of France issued a public protest against the deportation of Jews. The statement endorsed the efforts of Pastor Marc Boegner, president of the Protestant Federation of France, and declared that the church could not remain silent while thousands of human beings who had sought refuge in France were being persecuted.
Boegner had confronted Vichy premier Pierre Laval earlier that month over the deportation of Jewish children. He offered alternatives that would allow the children to remain in France, but Laval refused. According to Boegner’s account, Laval insisted that “not one of them must remain in France.”
The protest was later read from Protestant pulpits across France. Some Protestant communities, pastors, and relief organizations went beyond public declarations, hiding Jewish children, producing false documents, and helping families escape. Boegner was later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations.

September 22–24, 1943—Members of the Waffen-SS division Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler murdered Jewish families and refugees at several locations around Lake Maggiore in German-occupied northern Italy.
At the Hotel Meina, sixteen Jewish men, women, and children were taken away in small groups, shot, and thrown into the lake. Jews were also murdered at Baveno and Stresa. Some bodies resurfaced, making concealment of the crime impossible.
These killings formed part of the first organized SS massacre of Jews on Italian territory following Germany’s occupation of northern and central Italy. They demonstrated how quickly persecution escalated after Italy’s armistice: within weeks, German forces had begun identifying, arresting, and murdering Jews who had sought safety there.

text:
THE ENGLISH THAT ISN'T FOR YOU

Three o'clock in the afternoon. A small, cramped English school on Second Road, wedged awkwardly between a massage parlor and a laundry service. The air conditioning unit is losing its battle against the afternoon heat, leaving a ceiling fan to push the heavy air around in lazy circles.

Written on the whiteboard in black marker is a simple phrase: "What did you do yesterday?"

Five young women sit at cheap plastic desks. All of them are in their mid-twenties. All of them are from Isaan. They repeat the phrase in unison, their regional vowels wrapping heavily around the sharp English consonants, as if their native tongue is refusing to let the words go.

The teacher is a sixty-year-old Australian retiree. He isn’t doing this for the money. He does it because he genuinely "wants to help." He gently corrects their pronunciation, offers a warm smile, and says, "Good. Again."

One of the women glances down at her phone as it lights up. It’s her mother calling from the village. She ignores it. She is in an English class. She is busy learning how to be someone else.

Resting on the desk next to her phone is a notebook. Stuck to the cover is a white decal with a black "PU" logo. She doesn’t actually know what it means. A friend gave it to her, claiming it was some new brand, and she just stuck it on.

To understand what is really happening in this room, you have to understand that Isaan is not just a geographical region in Thailand. It is a social tag. A third of the country's population lives there, yet the region produces less than nine percent of the GDP. The average household income is roughly a third of what it is in Bangkok. This isn't a geographical accident; it is a rigid economic structure.

The Isaan dialect is a permanent class marker. When a woman from the Northeast speaks Central Thai, the accent lingers. Bangkok hears it immediately. It’s the reason a taxi driver in the capital might refuse a fare, or office workers might quietly mock a pronunciation. It is a stigma that she carries in her throat.

For her, learning English isn't about cultural exchange. It is an instrument of vertical mobility.

The Bangkok middle class respects English. They fear it, and they want it, because English is the language of the foreigner, the client, and the capital. When an Isaan woman speaks English, she is temporarily adopting the language of the people who sit at the very top of the economic food chain. For the duration of a conversation or a financial negotiation, she effectively leapfrogs the domestic hierarchy. In English, she has no Isaan accent. In English, her dark skin and rural background don't register in the syntax. She ceases to be an "Isaan woman" and simply becomes a "Thai woman."

But there is a massive fracture between the English she learns in that sweaty classroom and the English she uses at work.

The school teaches respectable English. "What did you do yesterday?" "I went to the market." "I like reading books." It is a language of dignity.

The bar teaches something entirely different. "Buy me drink." "You want short time?" "Where you from?" It is the working language of the neon streets.

The school attempts to teach her how to be a person, while the bar trains her how to be a commodity. The school provides a sense of self-worth; the bar provides the cash she needs to survive. The tragedy is that she attends both, but neither curriculum actually solves her problem.

She isn't taking English classes to get better at working in a bar. She is taking them to escape it. She wants the vocabulary required to work at a hotel reception, a travel agency, or to marry a foreigner and leave the country entirely. But the respectable English she learns in the classroom is useless on Soi 6, and the transactional English she masters in the bar will never get her a job at the Hilton. She is trapped in a linguistic purgatory between two languages, neither of which actually belongs to her.

Tourists often look at a bar worker speaking fluent English and view it as a triumph, assuming the language has made her equal. It hasn't. It just recategorized her.

She is no longer just a poor girl from the provinces; she is now explicitly a "bar girl who speaks English." When an educated Bangkok Thai hears her particular brand of English, they don't think she is well-educated. They know exactly which ecosystem taught her those inflections. The tool she bought to escape the trap simply becomes the ultimate proof that she was in it.

Furthermore, her English doesn't actually grant her access to the Westerner's world. It merely gives her a job inside it. She can flirt, charm, and negotiate, but she cannot explain the crushing weight of family debt, the obligations of a rural daughter, or the fluctuating price of rice. The foreigner doesn't speak Isaan, and her English isn't deep enough to translate her soul. English is just a bridge that leads into a room where absolutely no one speaks her native language.

It is both a weapon and a cage. It gives her unprecedented power and a secret edge over the locals who can't speak it, but every English word she learns is ultimately acquired for someone else. She doesn't learn it for the joy of literature or self-expression. She learns it for the men who pay. She can only say what sells.

And the hardest part is that she can never truly go back. She isn't the same naive girl who stepped off the bus from Roi Et two years ago. She has seen too much of the foreigner's world and learned too much of his language. She is stuck in the transition.

Ten o'clock that same night. The bar is loud. She is sitting with a fifty-year-old German client, laughing at a joke she barely understood. She asks where he is from and immediately tells him she loves Germany, despite never having owned a passport. She knows exactly what he needs to hear, so she manufactures it flawlessly.

Her phone vibrates on the damp bar counter. It’s her mother again. She doesn't answer. She just flips the screen face down.

The German looks at her affectionately. "Your English is very good."

She flashes a flawless, rehearsed smile. "Thank you. I study."

He leans in a little closer. "You're not like the other girls."

She doesn't reply to that. She just keeps smiling. She has heard that exact phrase a hundred times before. She knows it isn't a genuine compliment. It’s just the psychological justification he uses to make her feel special so he can comfortably pay her more later. She knows exactly how the game is played.

But buried deep underneath the English, underneath the central Thai, there is another language. The one she dreams in. The one she uses when she finally calls her mother back in the morning. A language she will never, ever show to the man sitting across from her.

Because that language is not for him.

text:
Paddy procurement hit by DPC opening delays as the TVK government tightens farmland verification to prevent traders/touts from using farmers’ documents to sell produce at MSP.

Tamil Nadu’s offers Rs. 2750 procurement price for fine variety paddy, which is Rs 350 to Rs 400 higher per quintal than in other southern states. 

Hence from this KMF season (Sep.1st), TNCSC introduced an additional layer of verification by RDOs. The RDOs will scrutinise e-Adangal and other land-related documents submitted online by farmers for selling paddy at DPCs. So far, these documents were verified by Village Administrative Officers and officials posted at the DPCs. The additional verification has delayed the opening of DPCs in some districts affecting the pace of paddy procurement.

The RDO-level verification is expected to plug the scope for malpractice, including manipulation of e-Adangal records to falsely show paddy cultivation. The move is primarily aimed at preventing paddy procured from other states, as well as old stocks stored at rice mills from being brought to DPCs and sold at the minimum support price (MSP).
 
“The RDOs will have access to data from the Agriculture department, including details such as area under cultivation in each village, seed supply and other details. At the divisional level, we will now be able to ascertain whether the quantity of paddy arriving at DPCs is proportionate to the area officially recorded as cultivated,” said a TNCSC official.

Currently, paddy farmers submit details of their crop cultivation through the e-Adangal crop administration portal. After the Village Administrative Officer physically verifies the standing crop, the application is approved. Farmers then submit their Adangal, patta and other land documents, along with their bank passbook, at the DPCs to sell their produce. The payment is subsequently credited to their bank accounts directly within 10 days.

Sources said several traders associated with rice mills in Tamil Nadu and neighbouring states purchase paddy from debt-ridden farmers at around Rs 1,800 to Rs 2,000 per quintal and subsequently sell it at DPCs at the MSP, making a margin of nearly 30% to 40%.

text:
Kirby Smart is trying to get one of his receivers off the field. He cannot do it.

"I keep trying to take him off to save money and it's not working."

The player is London Humphreys, and this is the strangest NIL story of the year.

Humphreys grew up in Nashville and went to Christ Presbyterian Academy. He was a three star. His offers were Vanderbilt, Memphis, Middle Tennessee State and Minnesota.

He picked Vanderbilt, and as a true freshman in 2023 he scored in his college debut. Against Wake Forest he went for 109 yards and a touchdown and was named SEC Freshman of the Week.

He finished that season with 439 yards and four touchdowns. He made the SEC All Freshman team. He was one of three freshmen in the entire conference with four or more receiving touchdowns.

Then he transferred to Georgia.

And he basically stopped catching the ball.

In three seasons in Athens he has 35 catches. Total. 531 yards, six touchdowns.

This year, through three games, he has 2 catches for 11 yards.

Here is the part that makes it interesting.

Almost every NIL incentive in college football is tied to production. Catches. Yards. Touchdowns. Playing time on offense.

Humphreys has a clause in his deal that pays him more for special teams snaps.

Not returns. Coverage. The part of the game nobody wants.

So he fights to be out there on every one of them, and every one of them costs Georgia money, and his head coach cannot talk him out of it.

Against Arkansas he came free off the edge and blocked a punt in the third quarter. The ball traveled 14 yards.

Smart on him this week.

"He cares so much. He's the highest-character kid on the team. He's one of the best blockers."

And then the punchline.

"He's worth it."

Now the honest part. He is getting paid for this. It is an incentive, and it is working exactly the way an incentive is supposed to work.

But somebody had to agree to build the deal that way.

A kid who was All Freshman in the SEC at 18 looked at a roster full of five star receivers, understood he was not going to be the guy, and tied his money to the ugliest job on the field instead of transferring again.

He is a senior now. He says his job is teaching the young receivers how to do it.

Most guys chase the ball. This one chased the coverage unit.

text:
In Zimbabwe, I see organizations missing a significant opportunity to develop their own talent.

Fresh graduates will often arrive raw. They may look inexperienced and offer limited value in the short term. But that is precisely why employers should invest in formal, structured two year graduate development programmes. I would go even further. Start identifying talent while students are on attachment. Identify and hire the brightest and most promising students, then bring them back as graduate trainees after they complete their studies.

This works. I went through a graduate trainee programme myself soon after completing my degree. At IPC, since we started the company, I have never hired an experienced employee. We have consistently recruited fresh graduates and trained them. Many have developed into excellent consultants, and every year we see some of them being recruited by other organizations. I would obviously prefer to retain them, but the fact that the market wants them is evidence that the development model works.

Yes, there are shortcomings among some of our graduates, and I have already discussed these in previous posts. But employers cannot simply complain about the quality of graduates while doing little to develop them. You can play a major role in turning raw potential into productive talent. 

A structured graduate development programme gives young people the practical exposure, professional discipline, technical competence and business understanding they cannot be expected to arrive with on their first day of work.
The same applies to artisans and tradespeople.

 Post O Level apprenticeship programmes appear to have declined significantly, yet apprenticeship remains one of the most valuable routes for developing electricians, fitters, mechanics, boilermakers and other skilled trades.

 If we stop taking young people through apprenticeships, we should not be surprised when the country later complains about shortages of experienced artisans.
Zimbabwe has no shortage of raw talent. What we need are more employers with the foresight to identify that talent early, invest in it and develop it. 

Employers should be competing for the brightest and most promising students for attachment, graduates for structured trainee programmes and school leavers for apprenticeships.

Discover the heart of Ireland
Take your time on this Ireland tour, which explores the most acclaimed sights in the south and west, including the mountainous beauty of Connemara.

Tour start
Dublin

Tour end
Dublin

8 Days
7  Nights

Day 1: Dublin City Tour & Pearse Lyons Distillery

Your Irish adventure begins with a 2:00 PM departure from your hotel in Dún Laoghaire, a picturesque coastal suburb of Dublin. Enjoy a panoramic sightseeing tour of the capital, taking in landmarks such as O’Connell Street, elegant Georgian squares, and St. Stephen’s Green. Continue to Dublin’s historic Liberties district for a visit to the unique Pearse Lyons Distillery, housed within a restored church. Learn about the area's rich heritage, hear fascinating local stories, and enjoy a whiskey tasting. Return to your hotel for a welcome drink with fellow travelers before spending the evening at leisure to dine and explore independently.

Day 2: Sean’s Bar & Galway Walking Tour

Travel west to the vibrant city of Galway, known for its lively arts scene and rich cultural heritage. En route, stop at Sean’s Bar in Athlone, recognized as the oldest pub in Europe and serving visitors since 900 AD. Upon arrival in Galway, join a local guide for a walking tour through its medieval streets and bustling city center. Afterwards, enjoy free time to discover the city at your own pace before gathering with your group for dinner at the hotel. (B, D)

Day 3: Connemara, Killary Fjord Cruise & Kylemore Abbey

Experience the dramatic beauty of Connemara, where rolling hills, sparkling lakes, and vast peat bogs create one of Ireland’s most breathtaking landscapes. Enjoy a scenic catamaran cruise on Killary Harbour, Ireland’s only fjord (seasonal operation). Later, visit the stunning Kylemore Abbey, set beside a tranquil lakeshore, and explore its beautifully restored rooms, charming Gothic church, and Victorian Walled Gardens. Return to Galway for an evening at leisure. (B)

Day 4: Sheepdog Demonstration, Cliffs of Moher & Killarney

Journey south around Galway Bay and through the rugged limestone landscape of the Burren. Gain insight into traditional Irish farming with a captivating sheepdog demonstration. Continue to the spectacular Cliffs of Moher, towering 700 feet above the Atlantic Ocean. Cross the Shannon Estuary by ferry before arriving in Killarney. This evening, enjoy dinner and traditional Irish music and dance at the renowned Kate Kearney’s Cottage. (B, D)

Day 5: Jaunting Car Ride, Ring of Kerry & Kenmare

Step back in time with a traditional horse-drawn jaunting car ride through Killarney National Park to the picturesque Ross Castle on the shores of Lough Leane. Continue along the famed Ring of Kerry, one of Ireland’s most celebrated scenic routes, featuring dramatic coastal vistas and mountain landscapes. Stop at Moriarty’s in the Gap of Dunloe before visiting the colorful town of Kenmare, where you can browse local craft shops, galleries, and cafés. Return to Killarney for a free evening. (B)

Day 6: Blarney Castle, Dungarvan & Waterford

Travel through Ireland’s lush countryside to historic Blarney Castle. Kiss the legendary Blarney Stone or spend time exploring the castle grounds and gardens. Continue along the scenic southern coastline to the Marine Bar in Dungarvan for traditional music in a welcoming local setting. text:
Slightly longer piece , but may be worth a read , given the debate of General Category vs Reserved Category going on.....Do you agree or otherwise?
 
One Flag. One Standard. One Future.

Dear IITians (as also others)

Before we are General or Reserved, we are Indians. That is the only identity that will carry our country to Viksit Bharat 2047. A developed India will not be built by one group defeating another on campus groups. It will be built when every talented child — from a metro coaching centre and from a government school in a far block — can stand in the same laboratory and argue about a prototype, not about ancestry. Enemies of our country look for cracks. They want our students to see classmates as rivals. We must not gift them that advantage.

This is a look at two decades of public evidence on IITs, written with respect, without slogans, and with one aim: raise capability so high that the nation needs no permanent dual standard at its summit.

What twenty years of entrance data show

Reservation in IITs follows the constitutional matrix: about 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC-NCL, EWS, and the rest open. The entry bar is not the same. That is a fact, not an insult.

To reach JEE Advanced, the JEE Main cut-off has risen for every category since 2019, yet the gap remains wide. General has moved from roughly 90 percentile to over 93; OBC-NCL from the mid-70s toward 81; SC from the mid-50s toward 64; ST from the mid-40s toward 52.

In JEE Advanced itself, the qualifying mark for SC/ST lists is typically set near half the Common Rank List. Branch closing ranks repeat the pattern. A Computer Science seat at IIT Bombay that closes near CRL 60–70 in the open list closes far later in reserved lists. Analyses of a decade of scores have found ST and SC median marks still far below the open-category median. At the present rate of catch-up, parity at the gate would take generations unless school quality changes.

This gap is not “lack of intelligence.” It is the compound interest of unequal schools, language, nutrition, coaching markets and social capital. An honest country names the gap so that it can close it.

What happens after they enter — and after they pass out

Inside the IITs, campus studies and institute analyses have repeatedly found average GPAs lower for SC/ST cohorts than for General and OBC students. In one well-known campus survey the GPA gap between General and SC/ST was about 0.84 points. An internal review at a leading IIT found that a large share of those with CPI below 5 were from SC/ST backgrounds. Parliamentary replies have shown reserved-category students over-represented among dropouts at several older IITs — in some years around three-fifths of undergraduate dropouts at the top seven IITs, though they are about half the intake. Official reasons include academic mismatch, wrong branch choice, health and other opportunities. Students and researchers also report isolation and the cruel campus habit of treating JEE rank as a caste test. Both can be true. A gap at the gate that is not repaired by teaching and dignity becomes a wound.

After the degree, the market is blunter and, in one sense, fairer. IITs have begun asking students to drop JEE ranks from placement CVs so that recruiters judge four years of work, not the exam that opened the door. Packages cluster by branch, CPI, internships and skill. Median domestic offers at older IITs commonly sit in the mid-to-high teens of lakhs; a thin tail of global tech and quant roles pulls averages higher. Category-wise salary tables are rarely published. That silence matters: once the degree is earned, employers buy competence.

text:
Harvey's economics have been widely reported, but some added detail helps set the context:

In May 2026, Harvey's CEO said the company was consuming roughly 13 trillion tokens per month. Bloomberg reported that Harvey's gross margin had fallen to -50% by June. At a -50% margin, cost of goods sold (COGS) is 1.5x revenue. Harvey passed $300M in ARR in June 2026, which implies roughly $450M in annual COGS. Assuming nearly all of that is inference, and spreading it across about 156 trillion tokens a year, Harvey's inference cost works out to roughly $2.90 per million tokens.

This explains why Harvey post-trained its own model, Harvey Tenet, on Moonshot's open-weight Kimi K3. The broader goal is to help law firms and enterprise clients build and own their intelligence, including their proprietary workflows. According to Bloomberg, Harvey's gross margin turned positive again after Tenet launched in August.

So why is Harvey the canary in the coal mine? There are three reasons:

Harvey is the most recent, and likely the clearest, example of LLMs being commodities.

An AI-native SaaS company chose to post-train an open-weight model, mainly because the unit economics of the frontier labs (e.g., OpenAI and Anthropic) are too expensive. This puts significant pressure on the valuations of OpenAI's and Anthropic's anticipated IPOs. Both labs have also just released new models: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol. Both are pitched as much cheaper than the models they replace, while matching or beating them on performance.

Pivoting Away from the Application Layer

Harvey's CEO recently talked about helping firms build their own AI systems. This marks a shift from an "application layer company" to a full-stack AI company. Harvey frames this shift as a response to customers asking: "How do we own more parts of the stack?" and "Should we be training our own models?" What is more revealing is OpenAI's release of Astra for Law.

Combined with the first point, it becomes clear that the frontier labs are moving into verticals and tailoring their foundation models to specific industries and use cases. This can (and perhaps should) be read as a sign that the frontier labs have reached the same conclusion: LLMs are commodities. This leaves Harvey at a structural disadvantage against OpenAI.

OpenAI's marginal gross margin on API usage is estimated at roughly 75–80%. Harvey pays those API rates. So if Harvey charges customers the same price for the same usage, its margin is close to zero. This means OpenAI can easily undercut Harvey. It can offer subscriptions that include usage priced below API rates and still make a profit. Harvey cannot. With Astra for Law, OpenAI has shown that it is interested in the legal vertical and is actively building products that target it.

Harvey's own CEO has said its real competition is the foundation labs, not other legal tech companies. As a result, companies like Harvey are pushed further down the stack, toward harnesses and post-training. That may be where the opportunity is. But if one of the leading legal AI vendors is pivoting to become, effectively, a consultant rather than a SaaS business, the implications are significant.

The Real "SaaSpocalypse"

Harvey's situation shows that the so-called "SaaSpocalypse" is really concentrated in vertical SaaS. Horizontal SaaS platforms, such as Salesforce, are mostly systems of record. They give agents a canonical, deterministic source of truth, backed by years of debugging, audit trails, and compliance work. This is very hard to replace. Vertical SaaS, by contrast, is mostly encoded workflows, which AI can easily replicate.

Ultimately, Harvey shows that unit economics are now the most important part of the AI story. For vendors, the question is whether gross margins can survive heavy token usage while keeping customers happy. For customers, it is whether that token spend earns a return. Harvey itself may well be fine, but if its future lies in building custom harnesses and post-trained models for individual law firms, it risks looking less like a software company and more like a consulting firm, which is unlikely to be where the value accrues.

text:
Nvidia's AI chips can be rented by the hour, not just purchased, and a data firm called Silicon Data tracks those hourly rates for three generations: the A 100 from 2020, the H 100 from 2022, and the newest B 200. These rates matter beyond the rental market because they indicate what older chips are still worth. That matters to Big Tech. When Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, or Oracle buy chips, they don't record the entire cost in a single year. Instead, they spread it across the period they expect the chips to remain useful- typically five to six years. The longer that period, the lower the annual cost and the higher the reported profit. Critics such as Michael Burry argue that AI chips remain useful for only two to three years. If he's right, these companies are overstating profits by about $176 billion from 2026 to 2028. Rental prices offer the best real-time test of who's right.

If the critics were right, older chips should have become cheaper to rent. Over the past year, the opposite happened. The H100, now more than four years old, rents for about $ 2.53 an hour, roughly 40% more than a year ago. The reason was a shortage. AI agents and coding tools required far more computing power than expected; a jump in memory prices early this year delayed new servers, and by spring, every new chip scheduled to arrive through September had already been booked. With new chips sold out, buyers turned to older ones, driving rents higher. Even the six-year-old A 100 still rents for $ 1.129 an hour, only 9% below last summer. So far, that supports Big Tech's five- to six-year view.

That shortage is now beginning to ease. The H 100' s rent peaked in July and has since fallen about 7%. July was also when Nvidia began shipping Rubin, its next chip, which it says cuts the cost of running AI models by up to 10 times compared with Blackwell. Previously booked capacity is also beginning to arrive. A 7% decline isn't a collapse, but it is the first sign that the forces keeping older chips valuable are fading. Watch to see whether H 100 rents continue falling toward $2 and below as new chips arrive. If they do, the six- year assumption will start to look generous. The real test comes in 2028 to 2030, when today's chips are still on the books but earning far less.
